sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.text:
In recent years, with the increasing integration of renewable energy into power grids, 
the spatio-temporal mismatch between renewable energy generation and load demand 
has become increasingly prominent. Issues such as wind and solar curtailment as well as 
load shedding pose signi ﬁcant challenges to the secure operation of regional grids [1]. 
Flexibility supply-demand balance refers to the extent to which the ﬂexibility provided 
by various resources exceeds the ﬂexibility requirement, at any moment, over any 
timescale, and in any direction, exceeding a permissible threshold. As the penetration of 
renewable energy continues to rise, ﬂexibility is becoming the core and critical aspect of

system operational characteristics [2]. Confronted with the challenge of renewable energy 
ﬂuctuations spanning second-to-day timescales, short-term energy storage can safeguard 
instantaneous system security and stability, while long-term energy storage signiﬁcantly 
reduces wind/solar curtailment and load shedding. Consequently, investigating hybrid 
short- and long-term energy storage systems (ESSs) to overcome the temporal limitations 
of single-type storage and achieve ﬂexibility supply-demand matching across critical 
timescales is crucial to ensuring bo th the secure operation and enhanced ﬂexibility of 
high-penetration renewable energy systems. 
As a key approach to enhancing renewable energy accommodation capacity in high-
penetration systems, wind-PV-storage integrat ed system planning has been extensively 
studied regarding the collaborative conﬁguration of ﬂexibility resources. Zipeng Liang et 
al. proposed a planning framework based on a three-level structure involving 
bidirectional converters to enhance the re liability and robustness of hybrid AC/DC 
microgrid clusters with high renewable en ergy penetration [3]. Shutan Wu et al. 
considered the spatiotemporal ﬂexible resources and multi-network coupling eﬀects, and 
proposed a cyber-physical integrated planni ng model for distribution networks. They 
established a three-level planning model to iteratively solve the planning problem. Case 
studies veri ﬁed that the proposed scheme can e ﬀectively alleviate the issue of voltage 
surplus [4]. Dundun Li et al. considered that increased wind integration and coal-plant 
retirements would heighten operational pressures on power systems, proposing a three-
level robust ESS planning model to accommodate uncertainties in wind power investment 
and coal unit retirements [5]. Zongxiang Lu et al. established a quantitative index system 
for power system ﬂexibility and developed a collaborative ﬂexibility planning framework 
integrating source-grid-load-storage resour ces [6]. Xiaorong Zhu et al. explored a 
coordinated planning method for energy st orage and Soft Open Points (SOPs) in 
distribution networks, optimizing resource allocation using multi-timescale ﬂexibility 
indices [7]. Lijun Liu et al. introduced a joint planning model for long- and short-duration 
storage, employing a deep clustering algorithm to characterize annual chronological 
features [2]. Deukyoung Lee et al. proposed a novel integrated planning method for 
generators, transmission lines, and ESSs, using a two-stage Benders decomposition 
approach [8]. Yanda Huo et al. developed a lightweight data-driven planning model and 
quantiﬁed the demand function for HESS in new power systems based on production 
simulation [9]. However, the ﬂexibility resource synergy mechanism in the above 
literature is imperfect and does not fully integrate the dynamic response characteristics of 
multi-dimensional resources of source, network, load and storage. 
Energy storage systems possess the capability for bidirectional energy ﬂow, oﬀering 
advantages such as energy shifting capability, rapid response, and ﬂexible deployment. 
These a ttributes enable ESS to e ﬀectively alleviate power su pply pressure during peak 
load periods, optimize power ﬂow distribution, and enhance grid operational e ﬃciency. 
In recent years, extensive research on hybrid energy storage has been conducted. Rukang 
Wang et al. addressed the challenge of wind-PV farm output 
ﬂuctuations impacting grid 
stability by proposing a hybrid ESS strategy for mitigating composite power ﬂuctuations, 
speciﬁcally considering the complementary characteristics between wind and PV power 
generation [10]. Xin Wang et al. leverage d Multi-Agent Deep Reinforcement Learning 
(MADRL); they ﬁrst analyzed the relationship be tween output power and wake e ﬀects, 
subsequently establishing a power smoothing control model for multi-wind turbines and 
energy storage systems [11]. Yutong Li proposed a method termed Principal Component 
Analysis-based Incomplete Data Equivalence to build data-driven energy storage 
dispatch models under conditions of incomplete data [12]. Fatma Gül şen Erdinç 
introduced an innovative approach for real-time energy management in residential 
communities, simultaneously considering the utilization of solar PV and ESS while 
Energies 2025, 18, 4986 3 of 25 
 
 
targeting cost minimization as the optimization objective [13]. Notably, the existing 
literature primarily focuses on wind-storage or PV-storage integrated systems, exploring 
the construction of energy storage primarily to mitigate power ﬂuctuations from wind or 
solar sources. Relatively limited attention has been paid to research on conﬁguring large-
scale centralized energy storage systems within regional grids that host signi ﬁcant 
penetrations of both utility-scale photovoltaic and wind power generation. 
The fundamental principle of power decomposition for HESS involves separating 
ﬂuctuating power components by frequency, allocating components with di ﬀerent 
frequencies and amplitudes to distinct fo rms of energy storage for absorption [14]. 
Inappropriate allocation not only increases the burden on the storage system but also fails 
to achieve the complementary advantages of the hybrid system. To address this, 
researchers have adopted various optimization strategies combined with modal 
decomposition methods to decompose the total HESS power. Zeyu Ma et al. proposed a 
double-layer VMD strategy. To mitigate the mode mixing phenomenon in the secondary 
VMD layer, they incorporated energy entrop y thresholds to identify the demarcation 
point for separating high-frequency and low-frequency components, aiming to achieve a 
more precise power allocation strategy [15]. Jicheng Fang et al. combined VMD with the 
Wigner-Ville Distribution algorithm to decompose the net load of an industrial park 
system [16]. Taiying Zheng et al. introduced a method utilizing VMD to con ﬁgure the 
capacity of HESS participating in secondary frequency regulation [17]. Rongchuan Tang 
et al. proposed a VMD-ST-QF load freque ncy division strategy, enabling precise 
decomposition of chronological load curves into high-frequency and low-frequency 
components [18]. Xinbo Zhou et al. proposed an IBWO-VMD-TCN algorithm that utilizes 
VMD to decompose historical industrial load into multiple modal components for 
subsequent prediction [19]. Despite generating relatively e ﬀective power allocation 
strategies, these existing methods exhibit signi ﬁcant subjectivity in selecting key 
algorithm parameters and

sections.title: 2.1 Modeling
sections.text:
The conﬁguration of HESS can enhance the power supply ﬂexibility of regional grids. 
If a hybrid energy storage system with suﬃciently large power capacity is conﬁgured for 
renewable energy farms, it can functionally balance imbalances in ramp rate, power 
magnitude, and energy capacity. Howeve r, excessive energy storage capacity 
conﬁguration will lead to substantial unnecessary energy storage installation costs and 
operational maintenance costs, causing resource waste. 
The planning problem for energy storage encompasses economic and stability 
aspects. The economic aspect refers to the co sts throughout the entire lifecycle of energy 
storage, including investment costs, oper ational costs, and penalty costs for insu ﬃcient 
system ﬂexibility. The stability aspect includes two dimensions: one is ﬂexibility 
regulation capability, meaning the stabilizing e ﬀect of energy storage on net load 
ﬂuctuations; the other is the impact of ener gy storage operation on the distribution 
network, including voltage ﬂuctuations and line losses. The power system architecture is 
shown in Figure 1. 
 
Figure 1. Power grid system.

sections.title: 2.1.1 HESS Model
sections.text:
This chapter selects a ﬂow ba ttery–lithium-ion ba ttery energy storage system to 
address the system’s ﬂexibility requirements across di ﬀerent time scales. Flow ba tteries 
oﬀer long lifespan, rapid response, and adjustable capacity; di ﬀerent storage capacity 

Energies 2025, 18, 4986 5 of 25 
 
 
demands can be met by adjusting the concen tration and volume of the electrolyte. 
Lithium-ion ba tteries feature high energy density, response times in the millisecond 
range, and rapid response to ﬂexibility demands. In this study, the ﬂow ba ttery is 
conﬁgured as the long-duration ener gy storage and the lithium-ion ba ttery as the short-
duration energy storage. Compared to single-type energy storage systems, hybrid energy 
storage combines complementary advantages: it can frequently charge and discharge to 
smooth high-frequency ﬂuctuation components, while also possessing large capacity to 
smooth low-frequency ﬂuctuation components with signi ﬁcant energy magnitude, 
oﬀering superior economic eﬃciency and performance. This paper employs an improved 
VMD algorithm to decompose the power of the energy storage system, generating power 
signals for the ﬂow battery and lithium-ion battery within the system. 
VMD originates from the Empirical Mode Decomposition (EMD) algorithm. Both 
algorithms can decompose a signal into multiple local oscillatory modes [20]. However, 
VMD exhibits signi ﬁcant advantages: it is fundamen tally grounded in optimization 
theory, enabling the mathematical description of signals within a variational framework; 
this ensures unique decomposition results and provides strong adaptability for non-
stationary signals. VMD e ﬀectively mitigates the common issues in EMD and similar 
algorithms, such as mode mixing and endpoint e ﬀects. It is particularly suitable for 
processing signals exhibiting signi ﬁcant local frequency variations and demonstrates 
favorable local characteristics in time-frequency distributions. Consequently, VMD has 
found widespread application across various domains including signal processing, image 
processing, and machine learning. 
VMD decomposition aims to identify K intrinsic mode functions

The VMD algorithm decomposes the total energy storage target output into K modal 
components across different frequency bands. The ultimate goal is to identify an appropriate 
Energies 2025, 18, 4986 6 of 25 
 
 
frequency division point to reconstitute these modal components into high-frequency and 
low-frequency signal components, with the low-frequency component serving as the target 
power for lithium-ion batteries and the high-frequency component as the target power for 
flow batteries. When the number of frequency divisions KL is too high, it leads to excessive 
decomposition of the energy storage target output. In this case, the sum of the reconstructed 
components will be less than the actual energy storage target output. Under such 
circumstances, the actual output of the energy storage system cannot fully mitigate wind 
power fluctuations, resulting in poor mitigation performance of the energy storage system. 
In order to eﬀectively suppress the spectral over-decomposition phenomenon during 
the decomposition process and to maintain the physical integrity of the output 
characteristics of the energy storage system , this study proposes an improved energy 
storage power allocation method incorporating Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO):

sections.title: 2.1.5 Constraints
sections.text:
Considering the impact of centralized energy storage conﬁguration on grid stability, 
and combining the energy storage’s own charge–discharge balance constraint and 
operating power constraint, the following constraints are obtained: 
Excessive charging and discharging of the energy storage system will both lead to a 
substantial reduction in its cycle life. Di ﬀerent types of energy storage have di ﬀerent 
optimal capacity operating intervals. Limiting the operating interval of the energy storage 
capacity within the optimal interval can e ﬀectively increase the number of cycles and 
service life of the ba ttery. This paper focuses solely on capacity constraints for research, 
ignoring the energy attenuation of the energy storage during use.

sections.title: 3 Problem Description and Modeling Double-Layer Optimization
sections.text:
Conﬁguration Solution Process 
This study establishes a mixed-integer nonlinear bi-level optimization model for 
hybrid energy storage systems. The uppe r layer determines storage location, rated 
capacity, and rated power to minimize annualized lifecycle costs. The lower layer 
allocates storage power to optimize ﬂexibility regulation and voltage stability. Power 
signals are decomposed into high-frequency (lithium-ion ba tteries) and low-frequency 
(ﬂow ba tteries) components using frequency sepa ration. These results feed back to the 
upper layer for iterative re ﬁnement of capacity/power pla nning, creating a closed-loop 
between long-term planning and short-term operation. The Weighted Average Algorithm 
(WAA) solves both optimization layers. The solution process for hybrid energy storage 
double-layer optimization is shown in Figure 2.

sections.title: 3.1 Weighted Average Algorithm
sections.text:
In this paper, the upper level planning is a mixed integer nonlinear problem and the 
lower run is a non-convex optimization, which cannot be solved directly by traditional 
mathematical planning methods such as KKT conditions, and heuristic algorithms are 
commonly used for energy storage planning problems of similar complexity [22]. 
Weighted average algorithm (WAA) is a novel metaheuristic algorithm inspired by the 
concept of weighted average position. Unli ke previous swarm intelligence algorithms, 
this algorithm requires constructing the weighted average position of the entire 
population during each iteration, preventing individuals in the population from 
becoming trapped in local optima [23]. 
The main idea of the WAA is to apply the weighted average position to search for 
near-optimal solutions. When calculating the overall average position, it is necessary to 
consider the weights of each element in the da taset; elements with larger weights exert a 
more signiﬁcant inﬂuence on the ﬁnal average position.

sections.title: 3.2 Improvement Strategy
sections.text:
The standard WAA provides a robust foun dation for optimization but exhibits two 
primary limitations when solving the complex, high-dimensional bi-level HESS planning 
problem formulated in this study: 
In preliminary tests, the standard WAA occasionally converged to local optima, 
particularly when initial populations were distributed in less favorable regions of the 
search space. This is a ttributed to its exploitation-dominated search strategy in later 
stages, which lacks an eﬀective mechanism to escape local basins of attraction. 
For multi-objective optimization, maintaining a diverse and well-distributed set of 
non-dominated solutions is critical. The conventional crowding distance calculation, used 
for niching and selection, often fails to pres erve solution diversity uniformly across the 
objective space, especially with more than two objectives. To address these challenges, the 
Improved WAA (IWAA) incorporates two targeted strategies. 
3.2.1. Reﬂective Reverse Learning Strategy 
This paper introduces the re fraction opposition-based learning strategy into the 
second optimization approach of the WAA exploration phase. The refraction opposition-
based learning mechanism is an excellent improvement mechanism for optimizing initial 
assignments and candidate solutions. Buildi ng upon opposition-based learning, it 
combines the law of light refraction to search for the optimal solution, enabling the 
algorithm to jump out of the current optimiza tion position region and direction during 
the WAA exploration phase. The Equation is as follows:
